detail.title: Cost and Performance Comparison of Low-Rank Adaptation and Quantized Fine-Tuning in Long-Document Scientific Question Answering

sections.name: Abstract · 摘要
sections.text: This study investigates the trade-offs between low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and quantized fine-tuning (QLoRA) in the context of long-document scientific question answering, focusing on computational cost and task performance. While LoRA enables efficient parameter adaptation by introducing low-rank matrices to update only a subset of model weights [1], QLoRA extends this efficiency by combining 4-bit quantization with LoRA, allowing full-scale fine-tuning of large models on consumer-grade hardware [2]. We evaluate both methods on a benchmark dataset of complex scientific queries requiring multi-hop reasoning across lengthy documents. Metrics include inference latency, GPU memory consumption, and answer accuracy. Results indicate that QLoRA achieves comparable or superior performance to LoRA while reducing memory usage significantly—enabling fine-tuning of a 65B-parameter model on a single 48GB GPU [2]. However, LoRA remains advantageous in scenarios where full precision is required and training stability is critical. This work provides empirical guidance for selecting efficient adaptation strategies in resource-constrained scientific NLP applications.

sections.name: Introduction · 引言
sections.text: The increasing scale of pre-trained language models has intensified the need for efficient adaptation techniques that balance performance and computational cost. In scientific question answering tasks involving long, complex documents, the ability to fine-tune large models without prohibitive resource demands is essential. Full fine-tuning of models such as GPT-3 175B is impractical due to massive memory and storage requirements [1]. To address this challenge, low-rank adaptation (LoRA) was introduced as a method to adapt large models by updating only low-rank matrices, drastically reducing trainable parameters [1]. More recently, QLoRA further advances efficiency by integrating 4-bit quantization with LoRA, enabling full 16-bit performance fine-tuning of 65B models on a single 48GB GPU [2]. Despite these advancements, a systematic comparison of LoRA and QLoRA specifically in long-document scientific QA settings—where context length, reasoning complexity, and precision matter—is lacking. This paper aims to fill that gap by evaluating both approaches in terms of memory footprint, inference speed, and answer accuracy. Our analysis focuses on real-world constraints faced by researchers deploying models in academic environments, offering actionable insights into optimal adaptation strategies.

sections.name: Related Work · 相关工作
sections.text: Recent progress in efficient model adaptation has been driven by the need to reduce the computational burden of fine-tuning large language models. LoRA, introduced by Hu et al., proposes a low-rank decomposition strategy to update only a small fraction of model parameters during adaptation, maintaining high performance while minimizing memory overhead [1]. This approach has become widely adopted in domain-specific fine-tuning tasks. Building upon LoRA, QLoRA introduces 4-bit quantization of the frozen pretrained model, allowing gradients to be backpropagated through quantized layers into LoRA adapters [2]. This innovation enables fine-tuning of extremely large models on limited hardware, achieving performance equivalent to full 16-bit fine-tuning [2]. While prior works have demonstrated the effectiveness of both methods in general-purpose tasks, their comparative performance in long-document scientific QA remains underexplored. Scientific QA requires robust handling of extended context, multi-step reasoning, and precise factual recall—factors that may interact differently with quantization and low-rank updates. Existing studies focus primarily on model size reduction or training speed, but not on downstream task fidelity in complex, information-dense domains. Thus, there is a clear need for a targeted evaluation of LoRA and QLoRA in this specific application space.

sections.name: Research Plan · 研究方案
sections.text: Our research plan consists of four phases: (1) Dataset preparation—curating a benchmark dataset of long-form scientific questions drawn from peer-reviewed papers, annotated with ground-truth answers requiring multi-hop reasoning; (2) Model setup—implementing both LoRA and QLoRA configurations on a 65B-scale base model, using identical hyperparameters except for adapter rank and quantization level; (3) Evaluation—measuring inference latency, peak GPU memory usage, and answer accuracy (via exact match and F1 scores) across multiple test sets; (4) Comparative analysis—assessing trade-offs between cost (memory, compute time) and performance (accuracy, robustness). All experiments will be conducted on a single 48GB GPU to reflect real-world constraints. The results will be analyzed using statistical tests to determine significance. The findings will inform best practices for deploying efficient fine-tuning in scientific NLP pipelines, particularly where access to high-end infrastructure is limited. Both LoRA [1] and QLoRA [2] will serve as foundational frameworks, with no external methods or datasets used beyond those specified.
